title: Dating with Purpose and Covenant Mindset
subtitle: Moving beyond casual culture toward intentional relationship-building
summary: Dating culture often treats relationships as entertainment, swipe, match, date, repeat. But if marriage is your goal, you need a different approach: intentional dating that evaluates compatibility, builds connection wisely, and moves toward covenant commitment. This journey transforms how you date, from recreational to purposeful.

cover.heroImageDescription: A couple walking with clear direction, not wandering but moving purposefully together. Intentional, focused, hopeful.

targetOutcomes: Understand the difference between recreational and purposeful dating
Develop a covenant mindset that views dating as potential marriage preparation
Learn to evaluate compatibility in areas that actually matter for marriage
Pace dating appropriately, neither rushing nor drifting indefinitely
Make wise decisions about continuing or ending relationships
Prepare for the transition from dating to engagement

activities.title: The Problem with How We Date
activities.subtitle: Why modern dating culture produces broken hearts, not marriages
activities.whyThisMatters: Modern dating culture is designed for entertainment, not commitment. Swipe apps, casual relationships, and 'situationships' may feel exciting but rarely lead to lasting marriage. If you want a different outcome, you need a different approach.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Modern dating culture is designed for entertainment, not commitment. Swipe apps, casual relationships, and 'situationships' may feel exciting but rare...

cards.title: The Dating Culture Problem
cards.text:
Dating with purpose is not about pressure or timelines.
It is about approaching connection with clarity, intention, and reverence for covenant.

If you have ever dated on autopilot, hoping things would eventually work themselves out, this journey invites you to be intentional without becoming rigid or fearful.

Modern dating culture has serious problems:

**The abundance problem:** Infinite options create the illusion that someone better is always available. Commitment becomes harder when you're always wondering "what if?"

**The ambiguity problem:** "What are we?" Relationships drift without definition, leaving people unsure where they stand.

**The intensity-without-commitment problem:** Physical and emotional intimacy without corresponding commitment creates bonds that devastate when they break.

**The evaluation problem:** We evaluate based on chemistry and entertainment value rather than character and marriage readiness.

**The endless audition problem:** Dating becomes exhausting performances rather than genuine discovery.

cards.title: Recreational vs. Purposeful Dating
cards.text:
**Recreational dating** asks:
• "Is this fun?"
• "Am I entertained?"
• "Do I feel good right now?"
• "Where will this go? Who knows."

**Purposeful dating** asks:
• "Could this person be my spouse?"
• "Are we compatible in ways that matter for marriage?"
• "Is this relationship moving somewhere definite?"
• "How do I honor this person even if we don't end up together?"

Recreational dating optimizes for present enjoyment. Purposeful dating optimizes for future marriage.

cards.title: Your Dating Pattern
cards.text:
How would you describe your dating approach, more recreational or purposeful?

What has that approach produced? What would you want to change?

cards.title: Dating Can Be Different
cards.text:
You don't have to follow the culture.

You can date with intention, clarity, and purpose. You can evaluate what actually matters. You can pace things appropriately. You can communicate clearly about what you're looking for.

This isn't about rigid rules or sucking the joy out of dating. It's about alignment: if marriage is your goal, your dating should be shaped by that goal.

cards.title: A Prayer for Purpose
cards.text:
Lord, I don't want to date like the culture dates.

I want purpose, clarity, and direction. I want to honor the people I date even if we don't end up together. I want my dating to actually lead somewhere good.

Show me a better way.

Amen.

activities.title: Developing a Covenant Mindset
activities.subtitle: Viewing dating through the lens of lifelong commitment
activities.whyThisMatters: Marriage is a covenant, a binding, lifelong commitment. Dating is the evaluation process leading to this covenant. Understanding marriage as covenant changes how you evaluate, invest, and what you're ultimately looking for.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Marriage is a covenant, a binding, lifelong commitment. Dating is the evaluation process leading to this covenant. Understanding marriage as covenant c...

cards.title: What Covenant Means
cards.text:
A covenant is different from a contract.

**Contract:** "I'll keep my end as long as you keep yours. If you fail, I'm out."

**Covenant:** "I commit unconditionally. My commitment doesn't depend on your performance."

Biblical marriage is covenant. "Till death do us part." For better or worse. In sickness and health.

This is beautiful AND weighty. You're not promising to stay as long as you feel like it. You're binding yourself to another person for life.

This weight should affect how you date. You're looking for someone you can bind yourself to forever.

cards.title: What Covenant Mindset Changes
cards.text:
When you view dating through the lens of potential covenant:

**What you evaluate changes.** Not just attraction, but character. Not just chemistry, but compatibility over 50 years.

**How much you invest changes.** You don't give covenant-level investment to non-covenant relationships.

**How you pace changes.** You're not rushing, but you're also not drifting indefinitely.

**How you end things changes.** If the relationship isn't heading toward covenant, ending it is honest.

**How you treat the person changes.** You honor them as someone else's future spouse.

cards.title: Your Covenant Understanding
cards.text:
Have you thought about marriage as covenant before? How does this affect what you're looking for?

What would change in your dating if you truly viewed it as evaluation for covenant commitment?

cards.title: God's Covenant Love
cards.text:
Our understanding of covenant comes from God Himself.

God made a covenant with His people, unconditional, permanent, not based on performance.

"Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you.", Hebrews 13:5

Marriage is designed to reflect this covenant love. Husband and wife give each other a glimpse of God's unwavering commitment.

Dating with covenant mindset means looking for someone you can live out this picture with for life.

cards.title: A Prayer for Covenant Vision
cards.text:
Lord, help me see marriage the way You see it, as covenant.

Transform my dating to reflect this vision. Help me evaluate what matters for lifelong commitment.

I want to find someone I can reflect Your covenant love with for the rest of my life.

Amen.

activities.title: What Actually Matters for Marriage
activities.subtitle: Evaluating the things that predict lifetime happiness
activities.whyThisMatters: Dating culture evaluates the wrong things, chemistry, attraction, how they make you feel. But research shows different factors predict marriage success. Evaluating what actually matters helps you make wise decisions.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Dating culture evaluates the wrong things, chemistry, attraction, how they make you feel. But research shows different factors predict marriage success...

cards.title: What Culture Evaluates vs. What Matters
cards.text:
**What culture focuses on:**
• Physical attraction
• Chemistry and spark
• How they make you feel
• Shared interests and hobbies
• Status, income, lifestyle

**What actually predicts marriage success:**
• Character and integrity
• Shared core values
• Communication and conflict patterns
• Emotional maturity
• Spiritual alignment
• Family patterns and awareness
• Life vision compatibility
• Ability to restore after conflict

The first list isn't unimportant, attraction matters. But it's not enough.

cards.title: The Essential Evaluation Areas
cards.text:
Evaluate these areas thoroughly:

**1. Character:** Are they honest? Do they keep commitments? How do they treat people who can do nothing for them?

**2. Faith:** Where is God in their life? Is it growing? Do your spiritual lives align?

**3. Emotional Health:** Can they handle hard conversations? Do they manage emotions well?

**4. Communication:** Can you talk about difficult things? Do you feel heard?

**5. Conflict Style:** How do they fight? Can they restore? Do they take responsibility?

**6. Values Alignment:** Do you agree on faith, family, finances, lifestyle?

**7. Life Vision:** Are you heading the same direction?

cards.title: Seeing Dating Through a Covenant Lens
cards.text:
Think about someone you have dated or considered dating.

If you viewed this connection through a covenant mindset, not just attraction or convenience, what questions would matter more?

Write a few lines about how purpose, responsibility, and long-term faithfulness might change the way you approach dating choices.

cards.title: Your Must-Haves and Deal-Breakers
cards.text:
Write out your non-negotiables, important preferences, and deal-breakers.

Be specific. These become your evaluation framework.

cards.title: Character Over Chemistry
cards.text:
Here's a crucial truth: character over chemistry.

Chemistry fades. Attraction ebbs and flows. The spark can diminish with time.

But character is what you live with every day for 50 years. Integrity sustains you when feelings fluctuate.

"Charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting.", Proverbs 31:30

You want both attraction AND character. But if you have to choose, character matters more.

Marry someone whose character you deeply respect.

cards.title: A Prayer for Discernment
cards.text:
Lord, help me evaluate what actually matters.

Give me eyes to see character, not just chemistry. Help me prioritize what predicts lifelong happiness.

Guide my evaluation. Show me what to look for and what to avoid.

Amen.

activities.title: Pacing: Not Too Fast, Not Too Slow
activities.subtitle: Moving at a pace that allows wise evaluation
activities.whyThisMatters: Some people rush, engaged in six months with someone they barely know. Others drift, dating for years without moving toward commitment. Wise pacing allows genuine evaluation without either rushing or stagnating.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Some people rush, engaged in six months with someone they barely know. Others drift, dating for years without moving toward commitment. Wise pacing allo...

cards.title: The Dangers of Wrong Pacing
cards.text:
**Too fast:**
• Emotional investment before you really know them
• Physical intimacy clouding judgment
• Missing red flags in the excitement
• No time to observe character across contexts

**Too slow:**
• Taking without commitment
• Preventing growth because you won't commit
• Using someone's time while you waffle
• Fear disguised as "taking it slow"
• Drift without direction

Neither extreme serves the relationship.

cards.title: Healthy Pacing Guidelines
cards.text:
**First few months:**
• Getting to know character and values
• Light emotional sharing
• Physical boundaries maintained
• Deciding on exclusivity

**3-6 months:**
• Deeper conversations about life vision
• Meeting important people
• Addressing concerns that have emerged

**6-12 months:**
• Serious discussions about future
• Working through significant conflict
• Honest compatibility evaluation

**12-18 months:**
• Either moving toward engagement or ending
• Relationships shouldn't drift longer than this without clarity

cards.title: Your Pacing History
cards.text:
Do you tend to move too fast or too slow? What drives that pattern?

What would healthy pacing look like for your next relationship?

cards.title: Forward Movement Is Healthy
cards.text:
Healthy relationships move forward. Not recklessly fast, but steadily forward.

If a relationship is stagnating, same level of commitment for months or years, avoiding deeper conversations, that's a sign something is wrong.

Forward movement means:
• Growing deeper over time
• Increasing commitment matching increasing investment
• Having conversations about the future

Relationships that don't move forward usually end, they just take longer and hurt more.

cards.title: A Prayer for Wise Pace
cards.text:
Lord, help me pace relationships wisely.

Protect me from rushing into commitment I'm not ready for. Protect me from drifting without direction.

Give me courage to move forward and wisdom to know the right pace.

Amen.

activities.title: Intentional Dating Practices
activities.subtitle: Practical habits that lead toward marriage
activities.whyThisMatters: Purposeful dating isn't just a mindset, it requires practical habits. These practices help you evaluate clearly, maintain perspective, and move the relationship forward appropriately.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Purposeful dating isn't just a mindset, it requires practical habits. These practices help you evaluate clearly, maintain perspective, and move the rel...

cards.title: Practices That Change Dating
cards.text:
Intentional dating includes specific practices:

**Define the relationship clearly.** No ambiguity. If you're exclusive, say so.

**Date in varied contexts.** See them with family, under stress, in social settings, not just romantic dinners.

**Have the hard conversations.** Don't avoid topics because they're uncomfortable.

**Keep outside perspective.** Don't isolate. Keep trusted friends and mentors.

**Maintain your own life.** Don't make them your whole world.

**Evaluate regularly.** Periodically assess: Is this working? Where is this going?

cards.title: Questions to Ask Early
cards.text:
In the first few months, get clarity on:

• What are you looking for in dating? (Marriage? Something casual?)

• What role does faith play in your life?

• What's your relationship with your family like?

• What does your vision for the future look like?

• How do you handle conflict?

• What are your views on kids, finances, roles in marriage?

You don't have to ask these on date one. But don't wait until year two.

cards.title: Date Night vs. Real Life
cards.text:
Many couples only see each other in "date" contexts, romantic dinners, fun outings.

But marriage is mostly not that. Marriage is ordinary Tuesday evenings, stressful weeks, mundane tasks.

Intentional dating includes ordinary life:

• Running errands together
• Seeing them when tired or stressed
• Doing projects, not just activities
• Being around when life isn't Instagram-perfect

The person you marry is the person they are on ordinary days.

cards.title: Your Dating Practices
cards.text:
Which intentional practices do you need to adopt?

Are there hard conversations you've been avoiding?

cards.title: A Prayer for Intentionality
cards.text:
Lord, help me date with intention, not just drift with feelings.

Give me courage to ask hard questions. Help me see the person clearly across varied contexts.

May my practices lead toward wise decisions.

Amen.

activities.title: Navigating the Stages of Dating
activities.subtitle: What to do at each phase of the journey
activities.whyThisMatters: Dating moves through stages, and each stage has its own focus and challenges. Understanding where you are and what that stage requires helps you navigate wisely.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Dating moves through stages, and each stage has its own focus and challenges. Understanding where you are and what that stage requires helps you navig...

cards.title: The Stages of Purposeful Dating
cards.text:
**Stage 1: Initial Interest (1-3 dates)**
Focus: Basic compatibility check. Is there enough to invest more time?
Danger: Deciding too quickly based on one amazing date.

**Stage 2: Exploration (1-3 months)**
Focus: Getting to know character and values. Deciding on exclusivity.
Danger: Moving to intimacy before clarity.

**Stage 3: Deepening (3-9 months)**
Focus: Deeper evaluation. Meeting important people. Navigating conflict.
Danger: Ignoring red flags because you're invested.

**Stage 4: Decision (9-18 months)**
Focus: Is this the person? Moving toward engagement or ending.
Danger: Drifting without decision.

cards.title: What Each Stage Requires
cards.text:
**Initial Interest:**
• Stay light, don't over-invest emotionally
• Look for basic compatibility
• Ask: Is there enough here to keep exploring?

**Exploration:**
• Ask the important questions
• Observe them in different contexts
• Make clear decision about exclusivity

**Deepening:**
• Go through difficulty together
• Let them see your real self
• Meet family and important friends
• Address any concerns directly

**Decision:**
• Have honest conversations about marriage
• Make a decision, don't drift
• If it's not leading to marriage, end it honorably

cards.title: Your Stage History
cards.text:
In past relationships, which stages did you handle well? Where did you struggle?

What would you do differently knowing what each stage requires?

cards.title: Stage-Appropriate Questions
cards.text:
Questions for each stage:

**Early:** "What are you looking for?" "What's important to you?"

**Exploration:** "What's your family like?" "How do you handle conflict?" "What role does faith play?"

**Deepening:** "Where do you see us going?" "What concerns do you have?" "What would marriage with me look like?"

**Decision:** "Are we ready for engagement?" "What would need to change?" "Do we both see a future here?"

cards.title: A Prayer for Stage Wisdom
cards.text:
Lord, help me navigate each stage of dating with wisdom.

Help me not rush ahead or lag behind. Give me discernment for what each phase requires.

Guide me from initial interest all the way to covenant commitment, or show me clearly when to exit.

Amen.

activities.title: The Decision: Continue or End?
activities.subtitle: Making wise choices about the relationship's future
activities.whyThisMatters: Every dating relationship reaches decision points. Should you continue? Should you end it? Making these decisions well requires clarity about what you're looking for and honesty about what you're finding.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Every dating relationship reaches decision points. Should you continue? Should you end it? Making these decisions well requires clarity about what you...

cards.title: When to Continue
cards.text:
Continue when:

• Character is solid and consistent across time and contexts
• Values align on things that matter for marriage
• You're both growing spiritually
• Conflict gets resolved rather than repeated
• You genuinely enjoy being with them, not just the idea of them
• Trusted advisors affirm what you're seeing
• Peace about moving forward (not just excitement)
• They treat you with consistent respect and love
• Life vision is compatible
• You can be your authentic self with them

cards.title: When to End
cards.text:
End when:

• Character issues that don't improve despite awareness
• Core values don't align (especially faith, family, life direction)
• Red flags that you keep excusing
• Relationship brings more anxiety than peace
• You're staying out of fear (of being alone, of hurting them, of starting over)
• Trusted advisors consistently express concern
• You can't be yourself without negative reaction
• Conflict patterns are destructive and unrepaired
• You don't genuinely respect them
• You know it's not right but keep hoping it will change

Ending is hard. But continuing when you should end is worse.

cards.title: Your Decision Evaluation
cards.text:
If you're currently in a relationship, evaluate honestly: Which list does it match more closely?

If single, think about past relationships: Were there signs you should have ended sooner?

cards.title: The Courageous End
cards.text:
Nathan had been dating Laura for nearly two years. Everyone assumed they'd get engaged.

But Nathan had growing unease. Their values on faith didn't truly align, Laura said the right words but didn't live them. Conflict patterns weren't improving. He'd been excusing things for months.

Ending it was brutal. People didn't understand. Laura was devastated. Nathan wondered if he'd made a mistake.

But two years later, he married someone whose faith was genuine, whose character was consistent, whose values aligned. He was grateful he'd had the courage to end what wasn't right rather than settle into a lifetime of misalignment.

The courageous end made the right beginning possible.

cards.title: Clarity Is Kindness
cards.text:
Some people stay in relationships they know aren't right because ending seems "mean."

But continuing when you should end isn't kind, it's deceptive. It wastes their time. It delays their ability to find the right person.

Clarity is kindness.

If you know this isn't the person, ending it, though painful, is the most loving thing you can do for both of you.

"Wounds from a friend can be trusted.", Proverbs 27:6

The wound of an honest ending heals faster than the devastation of a relationship that should have ended years earlier.

cards.title: A Prayer for Decision Clarity
cards.text:
Lord, give me clarity about whether to continue or end.

If I should continue, confirm it. If I should end, give me courage.

Protect me from staying when I should leave. Protect me from leaving when I should stay. Make the right path clear.

Amen.

activities.title: Ending Relationships Honorably
activities.subtitle: When it's not the right person, how to exit with integrity
activities.whyThisMatters: Most dating relationships end, that's the nature of finding the right person. How you end matters. Ending well honors the person, maintains your integrity, and allows both of you to heal and move forward.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Most dating relationships end, that's the nature of finding the right person. How you end matters. Ending well honors the person, maintains your integr...

cards.title: Why How You End Matters
cards.text:
Poor endings leave damage:

• Ghosting leaves the other person confused and wounded
• Blame-shifting protects your ego but destroys their confidence
• Cruelty creates scars that affect their next relationship
• Prolonged ambiguity creates false hope and extended pain

Honorable endings:

• Provide clarity even though it hurts
• Take responsibility without being cruel
• Happen in person when possible (not text)
• Allow space for the other person's questions and feelings
• Remember they are someone's future spouse

cards.title: How to End Well
cards.text:
When ending a relationship:

**1. Be clear.** No mixed signals. No "maybe someday."

**2. Be honest but kind.** You don't need to list every flaw. Focus on incompatibility, not deficiency.

**3. Do it in person** when there's been significant investment. Text is for first dates, not relationships.

**4. Own your decision.** Don't blame them entirely or wait for them to end it.

**5. Allow response.** Let them ask questions and express feelings.

**6. Be firm.** Once decided, don't waver because you feel guilty.

**7. Create space.** After ending, give each other space to heal. Don't try to be best friends immediately.

cards.title: What to Say
cards.text:
Sample language:

"I've valued getting to know you, but I don't see this leading to marriage. I think we should end things."

"I've enjoyed our time together, but I don't think we're compatible in some important ways. I don't want to waste your time."

"This is hard for me to say, but I've realized we're not right for each other long-term. I want to be honest rather than let this continue."

**Don't say:**
• "Let's be friends" (not right now)
• "Maybe someday" (unless you mean it)
• "You'd be perfect for someone else" (painful platitude)
• "It's not you, it's me" (cliché that doesn't help)

cards.title: Your Ending History
cards.text:
How have you ended relationships in the past? How have relationships been ended with you?

What would you do differently knowing how to end well?

cards.title: A Prayer for Honorable Endings
cards.text:
Lord, when I need to end relationships, help me do it honorably.

Give me courage to be clear. Give me kindness to be gentle. Help me remember this person is precious to You.

May my endings leave people healed rather than harmed.

Amen.

activities.title: The Wisdom of Community
activities.subtitle: Involving others in your dating process
activities.whyThisMatters: Dating often happens in isolation, just you and the other person. But wise dating involves trusted community who can see what you can't, ask questions you won't think to ask, and provide perspective when emotions cloud judgment.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Dating often happens in isolation, just you and the other person. But wise dating involves trusted community who can see what you can't, ask questions...

cards.title: Why Community Matters in Dating
cards.text:
When you're in a relationship, you're not objective. You see what you want to see. You excuse what you shouldn't excuse.

Trusted community provides:

• **Perspective**, They see things you miss
• **History**, They know your patterns and blind spots
• **Objectivity**, They're not emotionally invested the same way
• **Accountability**, They can ask hard questions
• **Wisdom**, Especially those who've been married long and well

"Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.", Proverbs 15:22

cards.title: Who to Involve
cards.text:
Choose advisors who are:

**Trustworthy:** They can keep confidence

**Wise:** They have discernment, not just opinions

**Honest:** They'll tell you truth, not just what you want to hear

**Spiritually grounded:** They'll point you toward God's wisdom

**Experienced:** Especially valuable: happily married people

**Your advocates:** They want your best, not their agenda

This might include: mentors, parents (if wise), older married friends, pastors, close friends with good judgment.

cards.title: Building Your Counsel Team
cards.text:
Identify 2-4 people to involve in your dating decisions:

**1.** Name: _______________
• Why them? Wisdom they bring?

**2.** Name: _______________
• Why them? Perspective they offer?

**3.** Name: _______________
• Why them? Experience they have?

Commit to:
• Keeping them informed about significant relationships
• Asking their honest opinion
• Taking their concerns seriously

cards.title: Your Counsel Network
cards.text:
Who are the wise people you could involve in your dating process?

Have you isolated in past relationships? What happened as a result?

cards.title: A Prayer for Wise Counsel
cards.text:
Lord, I don't want to date in isolation.

Surround me with wise people who can see what I miss. Give me humility to listen to counsel. Protect me from my own blind spots.

Bring the right advisors into my life.

Amen.

activities.title: Spiritual Alignment: The Non-Negotiable
activities.subtitle: Why shared faith matters more than you think
activities.whyThisMatters: Scripture is clear: believers shouldn't be unequally yoked with unbelievers. But what does spiritual alignment actually look like? It's more than checking the "Christian" box, it's about shared direction, mutual growth, and unified purpose.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Scripture is clear: believers shouldn't be unequally yoked with unbelievers. But what does spiritual alignment actually look like? It's more than chec...

cards.title: Why This Matters So Much
cards.text:
Marriage involves your whole life, and faith shapes your whole life.

If you're not aligned spiritually:

• Where will you go to church? Will you go?
• How will you raise children spiritually?
• What will shape your major decisions?
• What happens when you need to forgive, sacrifice, or endure?
• Who will you turn to in crisis?
• What is the foundation of your marriage?

"Do not be yoked together with unbelievers.", 2 Corinthians 6:14

This isn't arbitrary restriction. It's wisdom. You're trying to build a life with someone heading a different direction.

cards.title: What to Look For
cards.text:
Spiritual alignment involves:

**Shared faith:** Both genuinely committed to following Christ, not just cultural Christians.

**Active growth:** Both pursuing spiritual maturity, reading Scripture, praying, connected to church.

**Similar conviction level:** If you're passionate about faith and they're lukewarm, that's misalignment.

**Compatible church values:** Not every denomination detail, but core beliefs and practice.

**Spiritual leadership willingness:** Especially for marriage, is he willing to lead spiritually?

**Mutual submission:** Both willing to submit to God's word even when hard.

Don't just look for the label "Christian." Look for living faith.

cards.title: Your Spiritual Requirements
cards.text:
What does spiritual alignment mean for you specifically?

What would you need to see in a partner's faith to feel aligned? What would concern you?

cards.title: The Missionary Dating Disaster
cards.text:
Kelsey started dating Marcus knowing he wasn't really committed to faith. But he was kind, funny, attractive, and said he was "open" to spiritual things.

"I'll help him grow," she thought.

Two years later, they were married. Five years later, she was going to church alone, raising kids in the faith without his support, and feeling deeply alone in the most important area of her life.

Marcus never became the spiritual leader she hoped. He resented her "pushing religion." Their core values diverged further over time.

"Missionary dating" rarely works. You can't change someone into spiritual maturity. Marry someone who's already there.

cards.title: A Prayer for Spiritual Unity
cards.text:
Lord, I want a partner who shares my faith, genuinely, not just nominally.

Protect me from the temptation to settle spiritually. Help me wait for someone I can grow with in You.

Bring someone whose heart is fully Yours.

Amen.

activities.title: Preparing for the Transition to Engagement
activities.subtitle: When dating has done its job and commitment is next
activities.whyThisMatters: If dating goes well, it leads to engagement. But how do you know you're ready? What should be resolved before making that commitment? This activity prepares you for the transition from dating to covenant commitment.

frameworkBasis.explanation: If dating goes well, it leads to engagement. But how do you know you're ready? What should be resolved before making that commitment? This activity pr...

cards.title: Signs You're Ready for Engagement
cards.text:
You may be ready for engagement when:

• You've seen each other in enough contexts to know who they really are
• You've navigated significant conflict and repaired well
• You've discussed the major life issues and align
• Trusted advisors affirm what you're seeing
• You have peace, not just excitement
• You've addressed the concerns that emerged during dating
• You want to do life with THIS person, not just be married
• Your spiritual alignment is clear and growing
• You can envision the hard seasons and still say yes

cards.title: What Should Be Resolved Before Engagement
cards.text:
Before getting engaged, resolve:

**Life vision:** Kids, career, location, lifestyle, are you heading the same direction?

**Family concerns:** If families have issues, have you addressed how you'll navigate them?

**Financial approach:** How will you handle money, debt, giving, spending?

**Roles and expectations:** What do you expect from each other in marriage?

**Deal-breaker issues:** Anything that's been lingering should be addressed

**Premarital counseling plan:** Agree to go through thorough preparation

Engagement isn't the time to figure these out. They should be resolved before you commit.

cards.title: Pre-Engagement Checklist
cards.text:
Before getting engaged, confirm:

□ We've discussed and align on faith and spiritual growth
□ We've discussed and align on children (want them? how many? how to raise them?)
□ We've discussed and align on finances
□ We've discussed and align on family involvement and boundaries
□ We've discussed roles and expectations in marriage
□ We've navigated conflict and know we can restore
□ We've seen each other under stress and in ordinary life
□ Our trusted advisors affirm this relationship
□ We're ready to commit to premarital counseling
□ We both have peace about moving forward

cards.title: Your Engagement Readiness
cards.text:
If you're in a relationship, evaluate: Which checklist items have you covered? Which still need attention?

If single, what do you now know needs to be resolved before engagement?

cards.title: A Prayer for Readiness
cards.text:
Lord, when the time comes for engagement, help me be truly ready.

Help me not rush before things are resolved. Help me not delay when it's clear.

Prepare my heart for covenant commitment. Confirm the right person and the right timing.

Amen.

activities.title: Your Purposeful Dating Commitment
activities.subtitle: Consolidating everything into how you'll date from now on
activities.whyThisMatters: You've learned a new approach to dating, purposeful rather than recreational, covenant-minded rather than casual. Now it's time to commit to this approach and let it shape every future relationship.

cards.title: What You've Built
cards.text:
Across this journey, you've developed:

• Understanding of dating culture's problems
• Covenant mindset for approaching relationships
• Evaluation criteria for what actually matters
• Pacing guidelines for healthy progression
• Intentional practices for dating well
• Stage navigation skills
• Decision-making framework for continue/end
• Honorable ending practices
• Community involvement wisdom
• Spiritual alignment as non-negotiable
• Engagement readiness criteria

This is a comprehensive approach to purposeful dating.

cards.title: Your Dating Transformation
cards.text:
What has shifted in how you see dating through this journey?

What will you do differently in your next relationship?

cards.title: Your Purposeful Dating Principles
cards.text:
Write your personal dating principles:

1. I will date with _____________ (purpose/intention)
2. I will evaluate _____________ (what criteria)
3. I will pace by _____________ (guidelines)
4. I will involve _____________ (which people)
5. I will maintain _____________ (what boundaries)
6. I will end relationships when _____________
7. I will be ready for engagement when _____________

Make these specific and owned.

cards.title: Dating with Hope
cards.text:
Purposeful dating isn't joyless dating. It's dating with hope.

Hope that you'll find the right person.
Hope that you can build something lasting.
Hope that covenant commitment is possible.

By dating wisely, you increase your chances of finding what you're looking for. You honor God in the process. You honor the people you date.

This isn't restriction. It's direction. And direction leads somewhere good.

cards.title: A Prayer of Commitment
cards.text:
Lord, I commit to dating with purpose.

I will seek covenant, not entertainment. I will evaluate character over chemistry. I will pace wisely and involve community.

Guide me to the right person at the right time. Help me honor You and others in every step.

I trust You with my relationship future.

Amen.

cards.title: Your Declaration
cards.text:
Declare this over your dating life:

"I will date with purpose and covenant mindset.

I am not looking for entertainment, I am evaluating for lifelong partnership.

I will prioritize character over chemistry, though I want both.
I will pace wisely, neither rushing nor drifting.
I will involve community and stay accountable.
I will maintain my boundaries and standards.
I will be honest about continuing or ending.
I will require spiritual alignment.
I will prepare thoroughly for engagement.

My dating has direction. It leads toward covenant love."
